data_schema.title: USDA Directive Extraction Schema v2.1 (DR/DM)
data_schema.description: Extracts metadata and structured policy statements from 3000 series USDA Departmental Regulation (DR) or Departmental Manual (DM). Governing rules: (1) Any field described as verbatim must be copied character-for-character from the source document. Never paraphrase, merge, abbreviate, summarize, or insert ellipses. (2) Do not infer. If the source does not support an optional field, leave the field out entirely. Never return an empty string or a guess. (3) Only the label fields in policy_statements (statement_kind, statement_function, modal_use, normative_force, actor_basis) are interpretations. Every other field is quoted or copied from the document.

document_type.description: Type of document as printed in the header, such as 'Departmental Regulation' or 'Departmental Manual'.

issuing_organization.description: Organization issuing the document, verbatim from the header.

issuing_location.description: Location of the issuing organization, verbatim from the header.

regulation_number.description: Official document number from the header, verbatim, for example 'DR 3105-001'.

subject.description: Subject or title of the document, verbatim from the header.

issue_date.description: Issue date from the header, as written.

expiration_date.description: Expiration date from the header, as written. Leave out if none is printed.

opi.description: Office of Primary Interest (OPI) from the header, verbatim.

supersedes.description: The prior document this document supersedes. Take all values from the supersession paragraph in the body (usually under Special Instructions/Cancellations), NOT from the header. Leave the whole object out if the document supersedes nothing.

document_number.description: Number of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph. If it is identical to this document's own number, still copy it from the supersession paragraph, not the header.

document_title.description: Title of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

document_date.description: Date of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

scope.description: The text of the Scope section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Scope section.

purpose.description: The text of the Purpose section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Purpose section.

inquiries.description: Contact information from the Inquiries section. Leave out any property the document does not state; never return an empty string.

office.description: Office or division named for inquiries, verbatim. Leave out if the document names no office.

email.description: Email address given for inquiries, verbatim, without trailing punctuation. Leave out if none is given.

table_of_contents.description: Top-level entries of the printed table of contents, in order, including appendices. Return an empty list if the document prints no table of contents.

section_number.description: Section or appendix identifier as printed, for example '1.' or 'Appendix A'.

section_title.description: Section or appendix title as printed in the table of contents.

page.description: Page number exactly as printed in the table of contents, for example '2' or 'A-1'. Copy it even if the section actually starts on a different page. Leave out if no page number is printed.

actors.description: Registry of every distinct entity that the policy text names in an acting role. One entry per entity. Include every entity used as actor_name in policy_statements. Also include entities the document names in a role without being directed to act (mark those mentioned_only). Documents (bylaws, regulations, directives) are NEVER actors and must not appear here. Return an empty list if the document names no actors.

name.description: The entity's name exactly as written in the policy text, without a leading article ('the') and without a possessive. Keep a compound name intact if the document writes it as one phrase, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'. This is the join key used by actor_name in policy_statements, so spell it identically there.

components.description: ONLY for a name that joins separate entities with commas or 'and' (for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices' gives 'USDA Mission Areas', 'agencies', 'staff offices'). NEVER split a job title from the organization that qualifies it ('Director of IT, Office of the Inspector General' is ONE position), and never split an organization name from the position it modifies ('Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) Associate CIOs (ACIO)' is ONE group). Each component is a verbatim substring of the name. Leave out for single entities.

items.description: One verbatim component of a compound actor name.

actor_type.description: Kind of entity. Use exactly one of: position (a job title, singular or plural, for example 'USDA CIO' or 'Mission Area Assistant CIOs'), office (an organizational unit, for example 'OCIO Executive Secretariat'), council_or_body (a council, committee, board, or similar body), group (a category of organizations or units, not job titles, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'), external_entity (an entity outside the document's authority), program_or_system (an IT initiative, system, program, or project that the document says must act or conform).

binding_status.description: bound_by_this_document: the document directs, permits, or assigns a function or role to this entity and has authority over it. mentioned_only: the document names the entity but cannot or does not impose anything on it (for example a council or agency outside USDA that the document says a USDA body partners with).

policy_statements.description: Structured statements from the numbered body sections only (not the table of contents, not the appendices). RULES. (a) SENTENCES: emit one statement per sentence. If a paragraph has more than one sentence, give each its own statement with ids suffixed .s1, .s2, and so on. Abbreviations and legal citations ('U.S.C.', 'CFR', '§', 'et seq.') do not end a sentence. (b) LISTS: when text introduces a list (usually ends with a colon, for example 'The USDA CIO will:'), emit the introducing text as one statement with statement_kind 'lead_in', and emit EVERY item of the list as its own statement with statement_kind 'list_item' and parent_statement_id set to the id of the lead_in. Never skip list items, including lists of legal authorities. For a list inside a list, parent_statement_id is the immediate parent. (c) NEVER merge text from different sentences, paragraphs, or list items into one statement. (d) Copy text exactly; do not summarize. (e) PRONOUNS: when a sentence's subject is a pronoun ('It', 'Its', 'They') that refers to a named actor in the preceding sentence, resolve it: set actor_name to that actor and actor_basis to resolved_from_prior_sentence. (f) DOCUMENT AS SUBJECT: when the grammatical subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'), leave actor_name out; the entities the document acts on belong in target.

statement_id.description: Printed numbering path of the statement: section number, then paragraph letter, then item number in parentheses, for example '1', '3.a', '5.d.s2', '6.a(1)'. Add '.sN' only when a paragraph contains more than one sentence. Must be unique within the document.

statement_kind.description: standalone: a complete sentence that stands on its own. lead_in: text that introduces a list and is incomplete without its items. list_item: a list item that completes its lead_in.

parent_statement_id.description: Include ONLY when statement_kind is list_item: the statement_id of its immediate lead_in. For every other statement leave this field out entirely; never return an empty string.

section_number.description: Number of the section containing the statement, digits only, for example '6'.

section_title.description: Title of the section containing the statement, as shown in the table of contents, for example 'Roles and Responsibilities'.

source_text.description: VERBATIM text of this one sentence or list item exactly as printed, including trailing punctuation such as ':' or ';' and including any list-ending words such as 'and'. No paraphrase, no ellipses, no text from any other statement. For a list_item, give only the item's own text, not the lead_in.

statement_function.description: What the statement does. obligation: a required action or compliance requirement on an actor. responsibility: a standing duty or function assigned to an actor, including present-tense descriptions of what a body does. role_designation: assigns an entity to a role, for example membership or voting status. authority: names a legal source of authority or a grant of authority. scope: states what or whom the document applies to. purpose: states why the document or a body exists. definition: defines a term. condition: states a standalone triggering condition. exception: carves out an exception. savings_clause: states that the document does not displace existing authorities or delegations. effectivity: states when the document takes effect or how long it lasts. supersession: states that the document replaces another. classification_rule: states a rule that classifies something or applies a requirement when a status is met. reference: points to another document or location. inquiry: tells who may be contacted. container: use for every lead_in statement. other: none of the above.

modal_verb.description: The modal word or phrase of the statement's MAIN clause, exactly as written, for example 'will', 'can', 'may', 'must', 'shall', 'must not'. Ignore modals inside relative or subordinate clauses (for 'advises the USDA CIO on IT matters that may become IT investments', the 'may' is not the statement's modal). For a list_item whose own text has no modal, copy the modal from its lead_in. Leave out if the main clause has no modal.

modal_use.description: deontic: the main-clause modal directs, permits, or prohibits action by an actor (for example 'The Deputy CIO will serve', 'can direct questions'). predictive: the modal only states what will happen or remain true (for example 'It will remain in effect until superseded'). none: the main clause has no modal.

normative_force.description: mandatory: deontic 'will', 'shall', or 'must' directing an actor to act or to serve in a role. prohibitive: deontic 'must not', 'shall not', or 'may not'. permissive: deontic 'may' or 'can'. assigned: a present-tense statement with no deontic modal that assigns or describes a function, duty, or role of a named actor (for example 'The CIO Council advises the USDA CIO on...', 'It assesses the needs of...'); use it only when actor_name is present, and never for purpose statements. descriptive: everything else with no deontic force, including purpose, scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, references, authorities, definitions, and statements about the document itself or about other documents. not_applicable: use for every lead_in; its force is carried by its list_items.

actor_name.description: The entity directed to act, permitted to act, or assigned a function or role by this statement, spelled exactly as in the matching actors[].name. It must appear in source_text or in the lead_in's text (leading article removed); for a resolved pronoun, copy it from the antecedent sentence. Leave out when the statement binds no actor: scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, statements about documents (including bylaws), and any statement whose subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'). Never supply an actor that is not stated in the text or resolvable from the preceding sentence. Always leave out for lead_in statements.

actor_basis.description: Include ONLY when actor_name is present; otherwise leave this field out entirely. explicit_in_statement: the actor appears in this statement's own source_text. inherited_from_lead_in: the actor appears only in the lead_in that this list_item completes. resolved_from_prior_sentence: the subject is a pronoun resolved to the actor named in the preceding sentence.

target.description: VERBATIM phrase naming what the action is directed at or what the statement applies to, starting at the first word after any leading article ('a', 'an', 'the'). For a role_designation, the body or unit the role is within (for example 'CIO Council'). Leave out if none.

resulting_status.description: VERBATIM phrase naming the status or role that a role_designation or classification_rule confers, for example 'voting member' or 'advisory (non-voting) members'. Leave out for other statements.

conditions.description: VERBATIM phrases that restrict when or to what the statement applies, for example 'that the CIO Council designates as enterprise initiatives'. Do NOT treat a non-restrictive descriptive phrase set off by commas (for example 'appointed by the USDA CIO' in 'The Secretariat, appointed by the USDA CIO, will serve') as a condition. Leave out if there are none.

items.description: One verbatim condition phrase copied from source_text.

cross_references.description: Other documents, laws, or regulations cited in source_text, each copied verbatim as ONE entry per cited authority, including its code citation (for example 'The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 11101 et seq.' is one entry; for a list_item that is just a citation, the entry is the item text without the trailing ';' or 'and'). Never add a separate entry for a title that is part of the same citation (the words 'Chief Information Officer' after '7 CFR § 2.32'). Never list generic categories such as 'law' or 'Federal regulation'. Leave out if none.

acronyms.description: Acronyms and abbreviations listed in the acronym appendix, one entry per row, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no acronym appendix.

acronym.description: Acronym or abbreviation exactly as printed.

authorities_and_references.description: Entries of the Authorities and References appendix, one per entry, each copied verbatim, including any date, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no such appendix.

items.description: One appendix entry exactly as printed, joined across line breaks.

extract_result.subject: Vital Records Management Program
extract_result.opi: Office of the Chief Information Officer
extract_result.purpose: This regulation outlines the policies and responsibilities for identifying and protecting records necessary for USDA to continue its essential functions and activities during and following an emergency, disaster, or event that could cause the disruption of normal operations. It augments information in DR 1800-1, Departmental Emergency Programs Responsibilities and the USDA Headquarters Continuity of Operations (COOP) Plan. The primary authority for establishing a vital records management program within the Federal Government is 36 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Subchapter B – Records Management, Part 1223, Managing Vital Records.

policy_statements.source_text: Preservation of vital records is a government-wide requirement imposed through a variety of laws and facilitated by the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) guidance.
Each Federal agency is required by statute and by regulation to establish and maintain a vital records management program.
policy_statements.actor_name: Each Federal agency

policy_statements.source_text: An effective vital records management program is essential to successful records management.

Vital records include records and information necessary to continue the essential functions and activities of an agency in case of an emergency or disaster; and to protect the legal and financial rights of the agency, its employees, and the public.
USDA is committed to working with its employees to protect and safeguard vital records.
policy_statements.actor_name: USDA

policy_statements.source_text: This regulation sets forth USDA’s policy and responsibilities in developing a vital records management program.
The intent is to ensure that USDA critical records are identified, maintained and protected and no loss of critical information occurs during or after an emergency or disaster.
Each USDA agency and staff office head will establish a vital records management program in accordance with this regulation and DR 1800-1.
policy_statements.actor_name: Each USDA agency and staff office head

policy_statements.source_text: Each USDA agency and staff office head will select and safeguard records required to ensure the continuity of essential USDA functions during and following an emergency, disaster, or event that could cause the disruption of normal operations.

policy_statements.source_text: The identification and management of vital records is an essential part of the Federal agency’s emergency preparedness responsibility.

An agency must provide for the protection and accessibility of its vital records and information necessary to conduct its essential functions under all conditions at its normal operating sites, ERFs and Devolution Sites.
policy_statements.actor_name: agency
policy_statements.target: its vital records and information necessary to conduct its essential functions
conditions: under all conditions at its normal operating sites, ERFs and Devolution Sites

policy_statements.source_text: Agency and Staff Offices must also preserve as vital records evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations and other activities of the Government.
policy_statements.actor_name: Agency and Staff Offices
policy_statements.target: evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations and other activities of the Government

policy_statements.source_text: Designation of vital records is a discretionary decision based on the agency mission, emergency functions, and emergency plans of operations.
A document’s designation as a permanent record has no bearing on its designation as a vital record.
policy_statements.target: document’s designation as a permanent record

policy_statements.source_text: Vital records generally fall into one of two categories:
Type I Emergency Operating Records that are those records needed to resume and continue operations during an emergency or disaster.
They are also necessary for the resumption of normal operations after an emergency.
Records that are normally considered vital include, but are not limited to:
Statements of agency missions in an emergency;
Primary Mission Essential Functions (PMEFs) documentation;
Mission Essential Functions (MEFs) documentation;
Delegations of authority and Orders of Succession;
Regulations or announcements to be issued immediately at the beginning or end of an emergency or disaster;
Lists of employees assigned emergency duties;
Information concerning the whereabouts of vital records;
Building plans;
Agency program records needed to carry out essential functions;
System manuals.
Staffing assignments and related policy or procedural records and standard operating procedures (SOPs);
Devolution Plans;
Reconstitution Plans.
Type II Legal and Financial Rights Records that are needed to re-create legal and financial operations, as well as to safeguard the interests of the organizations, its employees, and its clients.
Legal and Financial Rights records are not vital records unless the agency is the statutory office of record.
conditions: unless the agency is the statutory office of record

policy_statements.source_text: Legal and Financial Rights records include, but are not limited to:
Information about agency personnel, property, damage, and assessment data;
Fiscal records such as periodic summaries of financial status and records of monies received by and owed to the Government;
Accounts receivable and payable;
Land titles, leases and contracts;
Personnel Records;
Payroll Records;
Memoranda of Understanding;
Grant files;
Social Security records;
Payroll records;
Retirement records;
Insurance records;
Property management and inventory;
Any additional Legal and Financial Rights Records considered critical for continued performance of essential functions.
Mirroring these two types of vital records, a vital records management program should enable accomplishment of two things.
policy_statements.actor_name: vital records management program

policy_statements.source_text: First, the program will provide a USDA agency with the information needed to conduct business under other than normal operating conditions and to resume normal business afterwards.
policy_statements.actor_name: program

policy_statements.source_text: Second, the program enables agency officials to identify and protect the most important records relating to the legal and financial rights of the agency and those affected by the agency’s actions.
policy_statements.actor_name: program

policy_statements.source_text: An agency’s program should meet its needs during an emergency, within budgetary limitations.
policy_statements.actor_name: agency’s program
conditions: during an emergency, within budgetary limitations

policy_statements.source_text: The cost and complexity of ensuring the availability of every document that might conceivably be needed in an emergency would be prohibitive.
In order to make a vital records inventory manageable and useful in an emergency, it is essential to distinguish between important records and truly vital records.
Therefore, only those records needed during and after an emergency should be designated as vital records.
policy_statements.target: only those records needed during and after an emergency

policy_statements.source_text: In selecting such records, agencies need to keep in mind that individuals using the records during an emergency may not be the same individuals who normally use them.
policy_statements.actor_name: agencies

policy_statements.source_text: Important records may support a business operation, but loss of such records will not stop mission-critical operations.
Records that are truly vital, by contrast, are essential for mission-critical, business operations and are irreplaceable.
That is, the contents of vital records cannot be recreated, and the operations supported by these records cannot be performed without them.
It is particularly important that the vital records program be kept practical because:
It is an essential part of the emergency preparedness program designed to ensure the continuity of the Department under the most adverse circumstances.
Overall preparedness may suffer if necessary information is not available when it is most needed; and
conditions: if necessary information is not available when it is most needed

policy_statements.source_text: This program must be kept current indefinitely.
If the program is overly elaborate, cumbersome, or costly, it will inevitably become outdated.
conditions: If the program is overly elaborate, cumbersome, or costly

policy_statements.source_text: The procedures for ensuring vital records are available must be routine.
Vital records will normally be maintained as duplicate copies of original records in paper or machine-readable form, whichever is most appropriate.

These copies can be stored at designated Emergency Relocation Facilities and Devolution Sites or other designated locations depending upon the size and volume of the records, the frequency with which records need updating, the costs involved, and any security precautions that must be applied.
Growth of automatic data processing systems has made it necessary to safeguard quantities of electronic media used for information storage.
If vital records are maintained on electronic media, a copy of the program manual or other information required to use the records should be stored with them.
policy_statements.target: copy of the program manual or other information required to use the records
conditions: If vital records are maintained on electronic media

policy_statements.source_text: Because of the fragile nature of information stored on electronic media, agencies must ensure that electronic media stored at vital records locations are protected against loss.
policy_statements.actor_name: agencies
policy_statements.target: electronic media stored at vital records locations

policy_statements.source_text: Such protection should consist of periodic recalls and inspections of these records.
policy_statements.target: periodic recalls and inspections of these records

policy_statements.source_text: Information stored on electronic media may have to be replaced, recopied, or in other ways restored if the inspection results in the detection of an unacceptable number of errors or if the equipment the records were originally created on changes.
conditions: if the inspection results in the detection of an unacceptable number of errors
if the equipment the records were originally created on changes

policy_statements.source_text: The major disadvantage of storing vital records in machine-readable form is that the equipment needed to access the information may not be available or may not be in working order in emergencies.
Contingency plans must provide for emergency processing at an alternate site and assure that needed records are available.
policy_statements.target: emergency processing at an alternate site

policy_statements.source_text: As records are duplicated, they should be properly indexed to ensure easy access to specific information.
conditions: As records are duplicated

policy_statements.source_text: Time is a crucial factor in reconstructing a database or a system of records that has been damaged or destroyed by a disaster.
Therefore, regular systematic indexing of all stored information is a necessity.
In choosing an off-site storage location, do not pick one too close to your office or building.
conditions: In choosing an off-site storage location

policy_statements.source_text: If duplicate records are stored too close, the same disaster that affects the original records may also destroy the duplicate records.
conditions: If duplicate records are stored too close

policy_statements.source_text: Locations where vital records will be stored must provide adequate protection and accessibility.
Records will be stored to ensure ease of access, retrieval, and control.

Classified records must be handled in accordance with DR 3440-001, USDA Classified National Security Information Program Regulations and DM 3440-001, USDA Classified National Security Information Program Manual.

DM 3440-001, USDA Classified National Security Information Program Manual

policy_statements.source_text: Federal Records Centers, regardless of geographic location, are available for agencies desiring to store their legal and financial rights records.
policy_statements.actor_name: Federal Records Centers

policy_statements.source_text: In addition to storage space for paper records, most Federal Records Centers have environmentally controlled space suitable for the storage of vital records on magnetic tape and photographic film.
policy_statements.actor_name: Federal Records Centers

policy_statements.source_text: Emergency operating records should be handled in accordance with each agency's internal emergency preparedness programs and forwarded to the Emergency Operating Facilities.
cross_references: each agency's internal emergency preparedness programs

policy_statements.source_text: All vital records, whether legal and financial rights or emergency operating records, must be periodically updated to ensure that they remain current, complete, and accessible.
Maintain original vital records specified in the USDA records disposition schedule.
policy_statements.target: original vital records specified in the USDA records disposition schedule

policy_statements.source_text: Delete duplicate copies of vital records stored in separate locations when obsolete or superseded, and replace with updated revisions.
policy_statements.target: duplicate copies of vital records stored in separate locations
conditions: when obsolete or superseded

policy_statements.source_text: Officials may not dispose of records prior to the authorized disposal date or retained beyond that date except in situations in which records might be relevant to pending or threatened litigation.

except in situations in which records might be relevant to pending or threatened litigation

policy_statements.source_text: Agency or Staff Office. A major line or program organization of the Department headed by an Administrator (or equivalent) who reports to the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, an Under or Assistant Secretary, or a General Officer.
Archive. A collection of non-current Federal records that has been removed permanently from an agency and transported physically (in an acceptable) format to NARA.
At that point, NARA assumes legal responsibility for the preservation of the records because of their continuing or enduring value.
policy_statements.actor_name: NARA

policy_statements.source_text: Department. The U.S. Department of Agriculture; also referred to as USDA.
Disaster. An unexpected occurrence inflicting widespread destruction and distress and having long-term adverse effects on agency operations.
Disposition. A comprehensive term that includes:
Destruction (disposal) of temporary records no longer needed for the conduct of business;
Transfer of inactive records to a Federal Records Center;
Transfer of permanent records, determined to have sufficient historical or other value to warrant continued preservation, to NARA; and,
Donation of temporary records to an eligible person or organization after the authorized retention period has expired and after NARA has approved the donation.
Emergency. A situation or occurrence that warrants immediate action to save lives and protect property, public health, and safety.
To some degree an emergency disrupts USDA operations.
Examples of an emergency are:
Natural Disaster
Man-made and Technological Hazards
Terrorism
Emergency Operating Records. Emergency operating records are those types of vital records essential to the continued functioning or reconstitution of an organization during and after an emergency.

Included are emergency plans and directive(s), orders of succession, delegations of authority, staffing assignments, selected program records needed to continue the most critical agency operations, as well as related policy or procedural records that assist agency staff in conducting operations under emergency conditions and for resuming normal operations after an emergency.

Information Accessibility. The application or configuration of Federal Information Processing resources in a manner that accommodates the functional limitations of individuals with disabilities so as to promote productivity and provide access to work-related or public information resources.
Information Systems. The organized collection, processing, transmission, and dissemination of information in accordance with defined procedures, whether automated or manual.

Legal and Financial Rights Records. Legal and financial rights records are that type of vital records essential to protect the legal and financial rights of the Government and of the individuals directly affected by its activities.
Examples include accounts receivable records, social security records, payroll records, retirement records, and insurance records.
These records were formerly defined as "rights-and-interests" records.

Litigation Hold. The obligation of agencies, managers, and individual employees to ensure the preservation of documentary materials that might be or might become relevant to pending or threatened litigation.
If the documentary material was created in electronic format, it must be preserved in that original native format (See DR 3090-001).
conditions: If the documentary material was created in electronic format

policy_statements.source_text: Metadata. Data that describe other data.
The term may also refer to any computer file or database that holds information about another database's structure, processing, changes, etc.
Data dictionaries and data repositories are examples of metadata.

Permanent Records. Records appraised by NARA as having sufficient historical or other value to warrant continued preservation by the Federal Government beyond the time they are needed for administrative, legal, or fiscal purposes.
Program Official. An official with primary responsibility for developing and/or implementing a policy, program, or function.

Records. Includes "All books, papers, maps, photographs, machine-readable materials, or other documentary materials, regardless of physical form or characteristics, made or received by an agency of the United States Government under Federal law or in connection with the transaction of public business and preserved or appropriate for preservation by that agency or its legitimate successor as evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations, or other activities of the Government or because of the informational value of data in them.

Library and museum material made or acquired and preserved solely for reference or exhibition purposes, extra copies of documents preserved only for convenience of reference, and stocks of publications and of processed documents are not included." (44 U.S.C. 3301).

Records Management. The planning, controlling, directing, organizing, training, promoting, and other managerial activities related to the creation, maintenance, use, and disposition of records to achieve adequate and proper documentation of Federal policies and transactions, and effective and economical management of agency operations.
Records Disposition Schedule. A document, approved by NARA, which provides authority for the final disposition of recurring or nonrecurring records.
Includes Standard Form 115, Request for Records Disposition Authority, and the General Records Schedules (GRS).
cross_references: Standard Form 115, Request for Records Disposition Authority

policy_statements.source_text: Records shall not be destroyed except as authorized by an approved records schedule.
conditions: except as authorized by an approved records schedule

policy_statements.source_text: Temporary Records. Records approved by NARA for disposal, either immediately or after a specified retention period.
Also called disposable records or nonpermanent records.
Trustworthiness of a Record. To demonstrate proof, records must have the qualities of trustworthiness, that is, records with the following characteristics:
Authenticity – an accurate account of an activity, transaction, or decision
Reliability – content can be trusted as a full and accurate representation
Integrity – an assurance that the information has not been changed subsequently
Usability – the information can be located, retrieved, presented, and interpreted

Vital Records. Essential agency records that are needed to meet operational responsibilities under national security emergencies or other emergency conditions (emergency operating records) or to protect the legal and financial rights of the Government and those affected by Government activities (legal and financial rights records).

36 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Subchapter B – Records Management, Part 1223, Managing Vital Records
Preservation of vital records is a government-wide requirement imposed through a variety of laws and facilitated by the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) guidance.
Each Federal agency is required by statute and by regulation to establish and maintain a vital records management program.
An effective vital records management program is essential to successful records management.

Vital records include records and information necessary to continue the essential functions and activities of an agency in case of an emergency or disaster; and to protect the legal and financial rights of the agency, its employees, and the public.
USDA is committed to working with its employees to protect and safeguard vital records.
This regulation sets forth USDA’s policy and responsibilities in developing a vital records management program.
The intent is to ensure that USDA critical records are identified, maintained and protected and no loss of critical information occurs during or after an emergency or disaster.
Each USDA agency and staff office head will establish a vital records management program in accordance with this regulation and DR 1800-1.

Fiscal records such as periodic summaries of financial status and records of monies received by and owed to the Government;
Any additional Legal and Financial Rights Records considered critical for continued performance of essential functions.
Mirroring these two types of vital records, a vital records management program should enable accomplishment of two things.
First, the program will provide a USDA agency with the information needed to conduct business under other than normal operating conditions and to resume normal business afterwards.
Second, the program enables agency officials to identify and protect the most important records relating to the legal and financial rights of the agency and those affected by the agency’s actions.
An agency’s program should meet its needs during an emergency, within budgetary limitations.
during an emergency, within budgetary limitations
The cost and complexity of ensuring the availability of every document that might conceivably be needed in an emergency would be prohibitive.
In order to make a vital records inventory manageable and useful in an emergency, it is essential to distinguish between important records and truly vital records.
Therefore, only those records needed during and after an emergency should be designated as vital records.
only those records needed during and after an emergency
In selecting such records, agencies need to keep in mind that individuals using the records during an emergency may not be the same individuals who normally use them.
Important records may support a business operation, but loss of such records will not stop mission-critical operations.
Records that are truly vital, by contrast, are essential for mission-critical, business operations and are irreplaceable.
That is, the contents of vital records cannot be recreated, and the operations supported by these records cannot be performed without them.
It is particularly important that the vital records program be kept practical because:
It is an essential part of the emergency preparedness program designed to ensure the continuity of the Department under the most adverse circumstances.
Overall preparedness may suffer if necessary information is not available when it is most needed; and
if necessary information is not available when it is most needed
This program must be kept current indefinitely.
If the program is overly elaborate, cumbersome, or costly, it will inevitably become outdated.
If the program is overly elaborate, cumbersome, or costly
The procedures for ensuring vital records are available must be routine.
Vital records will normally be maintained as duplicate copies of original records in paper or machine-readable form, whichever is most appropriate.

These copies can be stored at designated Emergency Relocation Facilities and Devolution Sites or other designated locations depending upon the size and volume of the records, the frequency with which records need updating, the costs involved, and any security precautions that must be applied.
Growth of automatic data processing systems has made it necessary to safeguard quantities of electronic media used for information storage.
If vital records are maintained on electronic media, a copy of the program manual or other information required to use the records should be stored with them.
copy of the program manual or other information required to use the records
If vital records are maintained on electronic media
Because of the fragile nature of information stored on electronic media, agencies must ensure that electronic media stored at vital records locations are protected against loss.
electronic media stored at vital records locations
Such protection should consist of periodic recalls and inspections of these records.
periodic recalls and inspections of these records

Information stored on electronic media may have to be replaced, recopied, or in other ways restored if the inspection results in the detection of an unacceptable number of errors or if the equipment the records were originally created on changes.
if the inspection results in the detection of an unacceptable number of errors
if the equipment the records were originally created on changes
The major disadvantage of storing vital records in machine-readable form is that the equipment needed to access the information may not be available or may not be in working order in emergencies.
Contingency plans must provide for emergency processing at an alternate site and assure that needed records are available.
emergency processing at an alternate site
As records are duplicated, they should be properly indexed to ensure easy access to specific information.
Time is a crucial factor in reconstructing a database or a system of records that has been damaged or destroyed by a disaster.
Therefore, regular systematic indexing of all stored information is a necessity.
In choosing an off-site storage location, do not pick one too close to your office or building.
In choosing an off-site storage location
If duplicate records are stored too close, the same disaster that affects the original records may also destroy the duplicate records.

Locations where vital records will be stored must provide adequate protection and accessibility.
Records will be stored to ensure ease of access, retrieval, and control.

Federal Records Centers, regardless of geographic location, are available for agencies desiring to store their legal and financial rights records.
In addition to storage space for paper records, most Federal Records Centers have environmentally controlled space suitable for the storage of vital records on magnetic tape and photographic film.
Emergency operating records should be handled in accordance with each agency's internal emergency preparedness programs and forwarded to the Emergency Operating Facilities.

** Agency or Staff Office .** A major line or program organization of the Department headed by an Administrator (or equivalent) who reports to the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, an Under or Assistant Secretary, or a General Officer.

** Archive .** A collection of non-current Federal records that has been removed permanently from an agency and transported physically (in an acceptable) format to NARA. At that point, NARA assumes legal responsibility for the preservation of the records because of their continuing or enduring value.
At that point, NARA assumes legal responsibility for the preservation of the records because of their continuing or enduring value.
Department .** The U.S. Department of Agriculture; also referred to as USDA
Disaster.  An unexpected occurrence inflicting widespread destruction and distress and having long-term adverse effects on agency operations.
Disposition.  A comprehensive term that includes:
Destruction (disposal) of temporary records no longer needed for the conduct of business;
Transfer of inactive records to a Federal Records Center;
Transfer of permanent records, determined to have sufficient historical or other value to warrant continued preservation, to NARA; and,
Donation of temporary records to an eligible person or organization after the authorized retention period has expired and after NARA has approved the donation.
Emergency.  A situation or occurrence that warrants immediate action to save lives and protect property, public health, and safety.
To some degree an emergency disrupts USDA operations.
Emergency Operating Records.  Emergency operating records are those types of vital records essential to the continued functioning or reconstitution of an organization during and after an emergency.

Included are emergency plans and directive(s), orders of succession, delegations of authority, staffing assignments, selected program records needed to continue the most critical agency operations, as well as related policy or procedural records that assist agency staff in conducting operations under emergency conditions and for resuming normal operations after an emergency.

Information Accessibility.  The application or configuration of Federal Information Processing resources in a manner that accommodates the functional limitations of individuals with disabilities so as to promote productivity and provide access to work-related or public information resources.
Information Systems.  The organized collection, processing, transmission, and dissemination of information in accordance with defined procedures, whether automated or manual.

Legal and Financial Rights Records.  Legal and financial rights records are that type of vital records essential to protect the legal and financial rights of the Government and of the individuals directly affected by its activities.

Litigation Hold . The obligation of agencies, managers, and individual employees to ensure the preservation of documentary materials that might be or might become relevant to pending or threatened litigation.
If the documentary material was created in electronic format, it must be preserved in that original native format (See DR 3090-001).
If the documentary material was created in electronic format
Metadata . Data that describe other data.
The term may also refer to any computer file or database that holds information about another database's structure, processing, changes, etc.
Data dictionaries and data repositories are examples of metadata.

Permanent Records . Records appraised by NARA as having sufficient historical or other value to warrant continued preservation by the Federal Government beyond the time they are needed for administrative, legal, or fiscal purposes.
Program Official . An official with primary responsibility for developing and/or implementing a policy, program, or function.

Records . Includes "All books, papers, maps, photographs, machine-readable materials, or other documentary materials, regardless of physical form or characteristics, made or received by an agency of the United States Government under Federal law or in connection with the transaction of public business and preserved or appropriate for preservation by that agency or its legitimate successor as evidence of the organization, functions, policies, decisions, procedures, operations, or other activities of the Government or because of the informational value of data in them.

Library and museum material made or acquired and preserved solely for reference or exhibition purposes, extra copies of documents preserved only for convenience of reference, and stocks of publications and of processed documents are not included." (44 U.S.C. 3301).

Records Management . The planning, controlling, directing, organizing, training, promoting, and other managerial activities related to the creation, maintenance, use, and disposition of records to achieve adequate and proper documentation of Federal policies and transactions, and effective and economical management of agency operations.
Records Disposition Schedule . A document, approved by NARA, which provides authority for the final disposition of recurring or nonrecurring records.
Includes Standard Form 115, Request for Records Disposition Authority, and the General Records Schedules (GRS).
Standard Form 115, Request for Records Disposition Authority
Records shall not be destroyed except as authorized by an approved records schedule.
except as authorized by an approved records schedule
Temporary Records . Records approved by NARA for disposal, either immediately or after a specified retention period.
Also called disposable records or nonpermanent records.
Trustworthiness of a Record . To demonstrate proof, records must have the qualities of trustworthiness, that is, records with the following characteristics:
Authenticity  – an accurate account of an activity, transaction, or decision
Reliability  – content can be trusted as a full and accurate representation
Integrity  – an assurance that the information has not been changed subsequently
Usability  – the information can be located, retrieved, presented, and interpreted

Vital Records . Essential agency records that are needed to meet operational responsibilities under national security emergencies or other emergency conditions (emergency operating records) or to protect the legal and financial rights of the Government and those affected by Government activities (legal and financial rights records).
